title: First 12-Month Opportunity Map and Tooling Playbook
author: Marina Patel
body:
Purpose

This playbook maps the first 12 months of a new Redwooder’s lifecycle and the intersection between role progression, compensation/benefit touchpoints, and internal tooling access. It is intended for new hires, hiring managers, people-ops partners, and engineering/product leads who run onboarding and early-career development.

Executive summary

- We treat the first 12 months as a single coherent program made of three phases: Ramp (0–3 months), Impact (3–9 months), and Advancement (9–12 months).
- Each phase has measurable outcomes (technical deliverables, collaboration signals, customer impact) and tool access milestones (workstation, repo access, observability, cost dashboards).
- Managers and people-ops share ownership: managers own role-level outcomes and mentor pairing; people-ops own compliance, access gating, compensation touchpoints, and program audits.

Quick navigation

1) Phase definitions and success criteria
2) Role ladder alignment and level checklist (how to map early performance to promotion readiness)
3) Benefits & perks calendar (what comes when)
4) Tooling access matrix and deprovision plan
5) Manager/mentor playbook for month 0–12
6) Quarterly / 12-month review rubric and templates
7) FAQs and exceptions

1) Phase definitions and success criteria\n
Ramp (Day 0–90):
- Objective: Enable baseline productivity and team integration.
- Success signals (pick at least 3): completion of first-issue ticket or primer project; pass of security & infra checklist; active participation in two team rituals (standup + design review).
- Operational gating: workstation provisioned (laptop + peripherals), VPN + SSO + company email, access to GitHub teams, Slack, Jira, expense card.

Impact (Month 3–9):
- Objective: Deliver reliable, measurable output and cross-team collaboration.
- Success signals: shipping two customer-impacting changes, owning a feature or operational runbook, receiving at least two peer recognitions.
- Operational gating: read access to per-route model telemetry in Redwood Console (observer role), entry to on-call rotation if IC-level requirement documented.

Advancement (Month 9–12):
- Objective: Demonstrate readiness for broader scope and responsibilities (mentorship, technical leadership, larger project ownership).
- Success signals: completed promotion readiness checklist items (see section 2), at least one aligned 1:1 development plan update, participation in a cross-functional initiative.

2) Role ladder alignment and level checklist

Overview: This section maps common early-career milestones to level expectations across Engineering and Product general ladders. Use this to calibrate 6–12 month promotion readiness conversations.

Example mapping table (use as guide):
| Level | Typical scope in first 12 months | Evidence required (examples) | Owner for assessment |
| L1 / Associate | Small scoped tasks; learns codebase | PRs with reviewer feedback; completed onboarding project | manager + tech lead |
| L2 / IC2 | Independent delivery on features; owns small postmortems | Feature rollout notes; unit test coverage; peer feedback | manager + discipline lead |
| L3 / Senior IC | Leads feature area; mentors junior ICs | Architecture doc; measurable impact on latency/cost; mentored 1+ IC | manager + engineering director |

Promotion-readiness checklist (select the appropriate level checklist and attach evidence links):
- Technical: code ownership story, architecture/concept doc, measured metric improvement, reliable release history.
- Collaboration: cross-team communications, documented tradeoffs, stakeholder alignment notes.
- Growth: learning plan updates, mentorship logs, evaluator feedback.

3) Benefits & perks calendar (what comes when)

We synchronize administrative benefit milestones to the operational phases so managers can cue conversations.

- Day 0–7: Health plan enrollment window email, commuter/remote stipend details, first payroll setup.
- Day 30: Eligibility for Wellness stipend and Employee Assistance Program (EAP) introduction.
- Day 90: Eligibility for equity vesting check-in (how to view cap table), first performance checkpoint conversation and eligibility for peer recognition nominations.
- Month 6: Parental leave counseling review and benefits Q&A session with people-ops.
- Month 12: Compensation review cycle window and long-term equity cliff check; mentor check-in for career planning.

Perk matrix (examples):
| Perk | When it starts | Notes |
| Home office stipend | Day 0–7 | Claim via Expenses portal; receipts required under $1,000 cap |
| Professional learning budget | Month 3 | Request via L&D form; pro-rated in first year |
| Conference allowance | Month 6 | Manager approval required; submit cost estimate 6 weeks prior |

4) Tooling access matrix and deprovision plan

Goal: Ensure new hires have exactly the tools they need when they need them, and that leavers are deprovisioned with minimal security risk. This section lists the most common systems and who approves access.

Access matrix (abbreviated):
- GitHub (repo access): Owner = hiring manager; approval = tech lead. Grant: Day 0–3.
- Redwood Console (observer -> writer): Owner = platform product lead; approval = manager + security policy. Grant: Day 7–30 depending on scope.
- Cloud console (read-only): Owner = infra team; approval = manager + infra reviewer. Grant: Month 1 if needed.
- PagerDuty / On-call: Owner = SRE lead; approval = manager + SRE onboarding. Grant: after documented runbook competency.
- Expense card: Owner = finance; approval = people-ops. Grant: Day 3–10.

Deprovision checklist (manager + people-ops):
1. Submit deprovision request ticket in IT portal.
2. Reassign active tasks in Jira and mark ownership.
3. Rotate any shared credentials and update runbooks.
4. Revoke cloud keys and GitHub access; verify in access audit.
5. Exit interview and final payroll setup.

5) Manager & mentor playbook for month 0–12

Managers should run a repeatable weekly cadence for new hires in the first 90 days and move to bi-weekly in months 3–9. Suggested cadence: Weekly 1:1 + weekly onboarding sync (first 12 weeks), asynchronous review notes in People Ops tool, monthly feedback pulse.

New-hire 90-day checklist for managers (short):
- Week 0: welcome 1:1, assign buddy, confirm workstation and access.
- Week 1–4: weekly goal setting; small PR reviews and pair programming sessions.
- Week 6: first formal health check (people-ops template).
- Week 8–10: first project owners meeting with stakeholders.
- Week 12: 90-day review and updated 6-month plan.

Mentor responsibilities:
- At least one 1:1 per week in the first month, then bi-weekly; provide code walkthroughs; share team norms; advocate for mentee during planning.

6) Quarterly / 12-month review rubric and templates

Use the following lens when assessing 6–12 month progress: Impact (40%), Ownership & Reliability (25%), Collaboration (20%), Growth Mindset (15%). Attach links to the templated forms in People Ops.

Suggested 12-month conversation structure:
1. Preparation: candidate self-assessment + manager notes (2 days ahead).
2. Calibration: manager collects feedback from 3 peers.
3. Review: 60-minute 1:1 to review rubric and agree next steps (promotion, growth plan, or focused development).
4. Follow-up: documented plan in People Ops with measurable actions and checkpoints.

Promotion packet contents (minimum):
- Role and level requested (string)
- Evidence links: 3–5 artifacts (PRs, runbooks, design docs)
- Impact metrics and customer outcomes
- At least two peer reviewers comments
- Manager recommendation and attached development plan

7) FAQs and exceptions

Q: What if a new hire needs delayed access for security reasons?
A: Use the temporary access policy: grant limited-time access with explicit reviewer and expiry date. Document in the access ticket.

Q: How do contractors fit this map?
A: Contractors follow a compressed variant: Ramp (0–14 days), Impact (14–90 days), and then milestone-based continuation. Benefits are prorated per contract terms and access follows least-privilege.

Exceptions policy: People-ops will approve exceptions for visa/relocation timings, parental accommodations, and security-limited hires. Exceptions must be documented with duration and risk mitigation steps.

8) Implementation runbook for people-ops and managers

Step-by-step (first 30 days):
1. Pre-start (people-ops): verify offer acceptance, set up payroll onboarding packet, schedule IT provisioning two business days before start.
2. Day 0 (manager + people-ops): welcome email template, assign buddy, confirm access plan.
3. Day 3–10 (IT): verify GitHub, Slack, Email, Expense card.
4. Week 2: run security orientation and compliance attestation.
5. Week 4: 30-day checkpoint with people-ops for any outstanding de-risking.

Escalation matrix (who to call):
- Access issues: IT Helpdesk -> People-Ops -> Security (if privileged access)
- Payroll/wage issues: Payroll -> People-Ops -> Finance
- Behavioral or performance concerns: Manager -> People-Ops -> HR partner

9) Templates and artifact examples (copyable)

- 90-day review template (paste into People Ops)
- Promotion evidence checklist (bullet list)
- Manager welcome email with onboarding schedule (paragraph block)

10) Appendix: audit & compliance notes

- All access grants are logged in the access audit system. People-ops will run quarterly spot checks for new hires and update the onboarding playbook accordingly.
- For hires in restricted regions we use the Private deployment onboarding checklist (see related page).

Document ownership and update cadence

- Owner: people-ops (Marina Patel)
- Review cadence: semi-annual or after any major policy change (security, payroll, benefits).

Feedback and improvements

Please file suggested edits as inline comments in Confluence or submit a playbook improvement ticket to the People-Ops backlog (label: onboarding-playbook).
